title: LiC12: Leading Hybrid Teams: Toggling Context Across Time, Space, and Power
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon argues that hybrid work fails not because people are insufficiently in the office but because organisations moved where bodies sit without redesigning how work and power flow. He reframes hybrid as a configuration problem across place, time, work type, power and a hidden fifth dimension, workforce segment. Using a worked case of a regional team and the Cynefin domains (Clear, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic) with Lewin's leadership styles, he says leaders should pick the kind of problem first and the medium and style second. He builds practical pillars of clarity, coherence, connection and fairness, and curiosity, warning against proximity bias and culturally narrow norms. The essay closes with a diagnostic that asks whether a model rewards visibility over value, and concludes that effective leadership has always been context-toggling.
points: Hybrid is a design problem across place, time, work type, power and workforce segment, not a question of office days.
Start with the kind of problem (Clear, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic) and let medium, rhythm and leadership style follow.
Complex work warrants deliberate co-location or well-facilitated high-bandwidth sessions, while Clear work should live in async channels.
Proximity to headquarters becomes proximity to power unless leaders deliberately counter it and bring edge staff into sensemaking.
The closing diagnostic asks whether you reward visibility or value, and whether you are treating design failures as personal resilience issues.
quotes: Hybrid isn’t failing because people aren’t in the office enough. It’s failing because most organisations changed where bodies sit without redesigning how work actually moves: across time zones, across Run/Serve/Change, across workforce segments, and—quietly but decisively—across lines of power.
They had changed where bodies were, without changing how work was designed, who carried which load, or how power flowed. Hybrid wasn’t a policy; it was a context they were ignoring.
Most “hybrid” operating models touch place a bit (“three anchor days”) and gesture vaguely at time (“core hours”), then stop. Work type, power, and workforce segment are treated as background noise.
If hybrid is going to work across workforce segments and cultures, it can’t just be California in the cloud. It has to be locally legible.
Hybrid hasn’t changed that. It has just made the contexts more numerous, more visible, and harder to fake.
